title: If the sea were ink
hookLine: if every tree were pens and the sea ink, with seven more seas, His words would not run out (31:27)

lines: A REED PEN, A KNIFE, A POT OF INK.
cards: Before printing, writing was physical. A calligrapher cut a pen from a reed, sharpened it with a knife, dipped, wrote a few words, dipped again. Ink was ground and mixed by hand, and it ran out.

A copy of the Qur'an could take months. Every scribe knew the pot running dry halfway through a line. Near its end, Surah Luqman takes that ordinary scribe's experience and stretches it until it breaks.

teach.h: EVERY TREE ON EARTH, A PEN.
teach.b: Pickthall: "And if all the trees in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to help it, (were ink), the words of Allah could not be exhausted. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Wise." Picture it.
Every forest, every orchard, every palm, cut into aqlam, reed pens.

teach.h: THE SEA, AND SEVEN MORE, AS INK.
teach.b: The ocean as the ink pot, and seven more oceans poured in behind it. The scribes write and write, the pens wear down, the seas go dry, and the words of God are still not finished.
Pickthall puts were ink in brackets because the Arabic leaves it out; the picture is clear enough without it.
Surah Al-Kahf has a shorter version of the image: if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would run out before His words did, even if We brought another like it. What are the words?
Commentators gave several answers: His knowledge, which has no edge; His commands, the be! by which everything comes into being; His wonders in creation, which no one could ever finish describing.
Seven, in Arabic, often works as a number of abundance, not a precise count. The verse isn't measuring; it's overwhelming.

teach.h: A FEW DROPS FROM THAT SEA.
teach.b: And it says something about every book, every sermon, every lesson, including this one: they're a few drops from that sea. Whatever has been said about God, there's always more.
For many Muslims that isn't a frustration but a comfort: the source never runs dry.

how: Muslims often recite 31:27 and 18:109 when speaking of the vastness of God's knowledge and words, and calligraphers have written the verse many times.

games.why: 31:27: the words of Allah could not be exhausted.

practice: Think of one thing in the world that amazes you, the color of a sky, a child's laugh, the way a wound closes, and find one word for it, on a scrap of paper or held in mind.
Look at the word, notice how much more there is that it doesn't say, and let that feel like abundance, not failure. If you pray, you can say subhan Allah over it.

wordCard.voice: Aqlam. Pens: Luqman's picture of every tree becoming one, and the sea, with seven more, as ink, and the words of God still not running out. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: pens, the plural of qalam, the reed pen; the trees become aqlam in 31:27.

carryVoice: Your line: the words don't run out. The seas would go dry first. Until tomorrow.
